entities.name: Church of the East
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of the East (ܥܕܬܐ ܕܡܕܢܚܐ, ʿĒḏtā ḏ-Maḏnḥā), also called the Nestorian Church or the Assyrian Church of the East — is one of the oldest Christian churches in the world, tracing its origins to the apostolic mission of Thomas and Thaddaeus to Mesopotamia in the 1st century CE and developing as the major Christian tradition of the Persian (Sasanian) Empire and subsequently spreading across Central Asia, India, and China, reaching the Tang Dynasty court in China in 635 CE and establishing Christianity in parts of Asia centuries before European missionary efforts.

The Church of the East's extraordinary medieval geographic expansion made it, at its height (roughly 8th-13th centuries), the world's most geographically extensive Christian denomination — with dioceses stretching from Mesopotamia (the theological and patriarchal center) across Persia, through Central Asia along the Silk Road, reaching China (the Nestorian Stele of Xi'an, 781 CE, documents its presence), India (the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala), and having communities among Mongol tribes. The Mongol Empire period saw the Church of the East particularly flourish, as several Mongol queens and generals were Eastern Christians.

The Mongol Empire's collapse and Timur's 14th-century massacres (particularly devastating for Eastern Christian communities) catastrophically reduced the Church of the East. The surviving community (primarily in the Urmia/Hakkari highlands region) suffered the Seyfo genocide in WWI and subsequent dispersal. The modern Assyrian Church of the East is the surviving remnant of this ancient tradition.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of the East — once Christianity's most geographically extensive denomination reaching China along the Silk Road, nearly destroyed by Timur and WWI genocide — is historically significant as one of Christianity's most ancient and geographically adventurous traditions, now reduced to a small remnant.
